Loyalty/Rewards and Other Monetary Scams: The Points Guy (Net Interest)
items.text:
**Here's an interesting (but dated) one... from the amazing Substack "Net Interest."**

I had occasion today to look through point and reward economics, and next to central banking or sex trafficking or whatever it must be one of the most despicable industries out there. It's well-known that loyalty cards/rewards schemes are fiat money-printing scams that, at best, saddles the user with a below-mininum wage job (https://stacker.news/items/869415).

...but it's good for the companies running these schemes. (Yea, no shit: the money printing/issuing was always great, and under shitty monetary regime there's an incentive for everyone to become a bank or a bank-like entity #[743123](https://stacker.news/items/743123), https://stacker.news/items/1329539)

It's a typical example where businesses do things **against the interest of their customer** (thus, it's dishonest) *while looking* like they're providing you with extra benefits. Somebody should call Lizzy (Warren!). (Also, it's one area where the European Union, in its infinite overlording wisdom, made a limiting regulation that was *actually good* for us Europooreans! By capping interchange fees, they basically outlawed rewards programs and saved/spared 500 million Europeans the time/necessary effort to play these silly money games.)

***

In the age of card networks and (FX) spreads (https://stacker.news/items/1586158) and costs to merchants, the COST and BENEFITS of these (Ponzi?) schemes become entirely intransparent where everyone, like in democracy, think they might get one over on someone else.

At best, it's a selection-biased gamble where **sophisticated consumers take advantage by optimizing the terms/conditions/value of the whole scheme vs naive consumers** who mistakenly believe they can/will win, while the house (as every properly set-up gamble) wins. The naive consumers will inevitably make some sort of error in their financial behavior (overdrafts, not enough spending, not maximizing rewards, too small fish such that annual fee eats up all other benefits).

The most well-known examples here are

* **bank deposits**: people hold too much cash at low-yielding bank accounts vs what they could/optimally should keep in higher-yielding savings accounts. The difference, while maaaybe sometimes convenient for the customer, end up in aggregate securing a massive windfall (=cheap financing) for the banks
* **life insurance products**: life insurance is usually priced very affordably and attractively for the buyer, which the insurance company isn't doing out of ignorance or stupidity but because they know from experience that some portion of the buyers (accidents, life circumstances changing, or just neglect) will let their policies lapse after having paid for a few years, meaning free money for the company, or worse, sell it back to the company at a great discount (=again, free money)

Here's the conclusion from a Fed paper on the subject from a few years ago:

> regardless of income, sophisticated individuals profit from reward credit cards at the expense of naïve consumers. To probe the underlying mechanisms, we exploit bank-initiated account limit increases at the card level and show that reward cards induce more spending, leaving naïve consumers with higher unpaid balances \[...]
> Naïve consumers might underestimate these payments and incur costs from usage. Sophisticated consumers, in contrast, might rake in the benefits while avoiding the payments and thus profit from usage

Here's the graph they use to display the idea (sorted by FICO scores, but the same point stands)

![](https://m.stacker.news/162147)

*tl;dr*, the area between the curves is larger on the negative side than the positive side, thus a) redistributing from naive to sophisticated, but more importantly b) makes the entire scam profitable to the company to run: What it has to pay the sophisticated winners is less than what they manage to extract from the idiot losers.

## The entire edifice is a combination of beggar-thy-neighbor and race to the bottom, with misperception and money illusion becoming key features.

From our pal Matt Levine in a recent Money Stuff piece

> banks make a lot of their money from depositor inattention: When interest rates go up, bank customers mostly don’t move their money, because it would be a pain, so banks can pay below-market interest rates on their deposits.
> You could have similar worries about life insurance, or annuities, or mortgages: Lots of financial products are built (and priced) based on assumptions about customer inattention.

The strategy is that you intentionally misprice (underprice) your service, banking on the fact that, in aggregate, enough people who opt in for this juicy, nice-looking offers will make enough errors that the few sophisticated customers who take perfect, optimized advantage of the mispricing won't cost the company.

***

ANYWAY, **Marc Rubenstein walks through the logic and economics of loyalty programs** and points(!) to some of the intricate cross-subsidized and legal/economic oddities with these programs:

> A key question in the whole points dynamic is how much partners pay for miles. Avios Group deferred revenue at a rate of 0.88 pence per point on the stock it issued in 2023, its highest rate in many years. The consumer value of points varies widely according to how they are used, but The Points Guy puts the value of Avios at around 1.2 pence per point, so the benefit to the consumer is clear. 
> Because the airline can adjust the redemption rate to encourage the use of rewards in ways that reduce their marginal cost, it is able to offer rewards to card issuers at a discount.2 In this way, reward programs can generate profits for both issuers and airlines while generating loyalty to both, a significant positive sum outcome.

## “By minting points, airline companies are able to lock in substantial cash flows.”

> Online points-monitoring sites posting point “valuation” tables on a regular basis because of course the offers change and of course the issuer of this fake, unusable money manipulate it to their advantage.
> The only problem is that competition has been driving up the rate at which card companies pay rewards. Over the last 12 months, American Express has paid out 1.07% of purchase volume in rewards, up from 0.80% ten years ago. Other card issuers have seen similar reward inflation. Capital One paid out 1.29% of purchase volume in 2022, up from 0.80% in 2013. And Discover paid out 1.43%, up from 0.94%. 
> American Express was initially exempt from the EU rules, so my British Airways co-branded card remained unaffected. In 2018, though, the courts brought Amex into line. Fortunately, American Express agreed to eat the cost. My BA Premium Plus card continues to pay 1.5 Avios points for every £1 spent, equivalent to around 1.8% on the basis of The Points Guy’s 1.2 pence per Avios valuation. I guess I do pay £250 per year for the privilege, and Amex likely bought the points at a steep discount (in particular the batch they acquired in 2020 to help the airline out of a liquidity squeeze).

JUST that gives us a few intransparent economic flows:

* First: The Amex bailout of BA during ‘rona, purchasing made-up points at cheap discount… even if Amex nominally loses \~1.3% per dollar of EU transactions, if what they hand over to the customer in rewards (=made-up BA money) was acquired at well below par, there’s still a profit in it for the card company.
* Second, to recoup the yearly card fee of 250 quid, a user needs to transact just below £14,000 a year, basically most of the discretionary card spending for a normal (Europoorean) person… and that’s not giving you pounds back, but made-up BA money you must do some additional trixing (in their webshops, for air fares, for lounge access or extra luggage etc) to benefit from.

## “there are clear subsidies at play. Someone, somewhere is subsidizing my points habit – no longer the merchant, it is now other BA or Amex customers. Indeed, such subsidies are the most controversial aspect to the model.”

I don't quite understand what this percentage is referring to (a larger share of Amex revenues are going back to users than before...?) but it seems to suggest that there is some sort of competitive pressure to close this rent-seeking gap

items.title: Why Were Victorian Elites so Effective? (Works in Progress Magazine, Sam Hughes)
items.text:
## Amazing (long) read, highly recommend

I like Works in Progress. *A lot*. It's a serious outlet for long-form journalism, and it (usually!) features writers whose minds are oriented correctly toward the future. (its editor-in-chief lost his mind during 'rona, so I've stayed away from reading/subscribing or even attempting to contribute... *but I'm often very tempted*)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160670)

## What's the Key For Success?

Work hard, long hours, education, 5am, cold plunges, diversity, pay your politicians well to avoid corruption *blah-blah*?

No, no:

> The elites of Victorian Britain operated differently. Their schools and universities were not terribly academic and had very little STEM. As adults, **they got up late, drank a lot, and spent a remarkable share of their waking hours partying.** They loved feasting, sports, holidays, dancing, and dressing up. Contrary to their stodgy reputation, they were probably a lot of fun.

> the elites of nineteenth-century Britain were, by their own lights, extremely successful. For much of the century, Britain was the richest country on Earth. Its companies dominated global commerce, industry and finance.

## In Defence of Debauchery

![](https://m.stacker.news/160674)

* **SCHOOLING:** while strict (early age, regulated times, single-sex away from family, corporal punishment), the values the English Victorian elite cultivated at boarding school were remarkably progressive: loyalty, internationalism, studies of the arts -- Latin and Ancient Greek --

Amazing:

> There was **resistance to the teaching of science, not because Victorians were hostile to science** in principle, but because they thought it **irrelevant to the kind of moral and cultural formation** that a school for gentlemen was supposed to provide.
> (By contrast, girls were not usually taught classics, meaning that, rather surprisingly, affluent Victorian girls generally followed a more modern curriculum than their brothers.)

While not obviously successful, it cultivated valuable skills:

> ...The most that can be said for Victorians’ classical education is perhaps that, like schooling in any difficult subject, it trained students in self-discipline, memorization, and applying rules.

And *this* we could definitely learn from today:

> Under such circumstances, it is perhaps unsurprising that the share of time spent in the classroom was relatively modest. At Rugby School, weeks were divided into three ‘full days’, three ‘half days’, and Sunday. On a full day, students spent about five hours in the classroom, compared with maybe two hours on a half day.  \[AND, importantly:] They also tended to be shorter than those of contemporary elite schools in France, Germany, or Italy, where the curriculum was normally more academically rigorous.

## "Victorians thought extremely highly of sports, believing that they instilled team spirit and endurance, fostered mutual loyalty, channeled energy and competitiveness, and taught men how to win and lose graciously."

One Loretto School headmaster described the school's priorities: **1) character, 2) physique,** 3) intelligence, 4) manners, 5) information. First time *brawns > brains, eh*

* **UNIVERSITIES**: Not much studying, plenty of "teambuilding"

I found *this* observation interesting:

![](https://m.stacker.news/160677)

> Oxbridge tutors believed overwhelmingly that the purpose of an undergraduate degree was not training for work nor even preparation for academic research, but rather a general moral and intellectual formation that would fit students for any professional role they might later pursue.

also:

> Fellowships were opened up to laymen in the later decades of the century, but **Oxford and Cambridge did not become world-leading research institutions until they were transformed by German scholars fleeing Nazism in the 1930s.** The dominance of Oxbridge in British culture was unusual: these institutions educated a much larger share of the elite than was the case for any two institutions in any other country

Fuck, these peeps just had *great* lives. (In some respects, Oxford life these days is very similar!)

![](https://m.stacker.news/160679)

* **ADULTHOOD**: Busy-busy-fucking busy bee... but not in the way you think

items.title: OpenBitcoin.com: A new bitcoin block explorer with guides tools and games
items.text:
I have been building a bitcoin block explorer and I feel it's good enough to show:

[https://openbitcoin.com](https://openbitcoin.com)

The site runs its own hardware, bitcoin node and address index. No third-party blockchain API used.

Inside the site:

- Explorer: blocks, transactions and addresses at root-level URLs. (very important, a feature I always wanted with other explorers, a quick easy way to query an address) For example you can type openbitcoin.com/block_number_here or openbitcoin.com/txid_here or openbitcoin.com/address_here to load the page instantly without visiting the site to use the search bar :)

- Node census (openbitcoin.com/nodes): reachable nodes counted by my own P2P crawler, 8,958 nodes from 92 countries last run.

- Rich list (openbitcoin.com/rich-list): top 10,000 addresses and balance distributions.

- Prices: spot price as a median of three exchanges, with a quick conversion tool on the front page.

- Tools: fee calculator, address validator, message verifier, QR generator, and key tools built to be downloaded and run offline.

- Guides: on confirmations, UTXOs, self-custody, stuck transactions and more. Newbie friendly.

- Games (openbitcoin.com/games): three arcade games built on real bitcoin mechanics, stack blocks, clear a mempool backlog, and a slot machine that plays the actual odds of guessing a private key.

The website is open source. What stays private is my server's operational layer.

Would appreciate any feedback, happy to contribute to the community.

items.title: Pleb Economist #15: Aleatoric vs. Epistemic Uncertainty
items.text:
This is a post I'd been thinking of making for a while.  It doesn't have a huge amount of practical application, but it does raise some interesting philosophical questions, and could affect how we think/talk about security in Bitcoin.

***

# Aleatoric vs Epistemic Uncertainty

![](https://m.stacker.news/164619)
*Pick a card, any card*

Statisticians / mathematicians / philosophers / scientists have two ways of talking about uncertainty: *aleatoric* uncertainty and *epistemic* uncertainty.

**Epistemic** uncertainty refers to uncertainty due to lack of knowledge. Consider a deck of cards. Which card is on top?  There's a single truthful answer, but we're uncertain what the answer is because we lack knowledge.

**Aleatoric** uncertainty refers to irreducible randomness in a process. If I shuffle the deck of cards and then reveal the top card, what card will I reveal?  There isn't a single answer.  The answer depends on a random process.  The uncertainty arises from the irreducible randomness of the shuffle, not from a lack of knowledge.

The distinction matters for modeling, and thus comes up in economics, finance, physics, and any field in which uncertainty factors into decision making. If uncertainty is epistemic, then perhaps our models can do better by collecting more data. But if uncertainty is aleatoric, then our models can only improve by modeling the randomization process better, not necessarily by gathering more information.

***

# Does Aleatoric Uncertainty Exist?

The trouble with aleatoric uncertainty is that a lot of what we call aleatoric uncertainty might actually be epistemic---we just need to know the information that collapses the uncertainty.

For example, the card shuffling process is perfectly predictable if we knew the initial configuration of the deck, and if we knew the precise movements of the shuffler's hands.

That which we called aleatoric---the card shuffling process---becomes epistemic, and the uncertainty isn't based on an inherently random process, but based on our lack of knowledge regarding the initial conditions of the deck and about the steps used in the shuffle.

***

# The Copenhagen Interpretation vs. Pilot Wave Theory

![](https://m.stacker.news/164622)
*John Bell, who proved that the universe isn't locally real*

So does aleatoric uncertainty exist?  Is there anything at all that's inherently random, where uncertainty isn't simply driven by hidden information?

According to the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics, the answer is yes. The Copenhagen school says that a particle doesn't have a definite position until you measure it; rather, the particle exists as a probability distribution that only resolves when you measure it, which means the resulting outcome is inherently random.

But the Copenhagen interpretation isn't the only possible interpretation of quantum mechanics. There are others, including ones which collapse the quantum equations from aleatoric to epistemic uncertainty. One such example is "Pilot Wave Theory", championed by Louis de Broglie, David Bohm, and John Bell, which posits that particles have *definite* positions, but that a global "pilot wave" guides their movements in such a way that it results in all the same predictions of standard quantum mechanics. In this theory, if both the pilot wavefunction and the initial conditions of particles are known, then their positions can be perfectly predicted. In this interpretation, there is no aleatoric uncertainty, only epistemic.

So, does aleatoric uncertainty actually exist?  The answer is, it depends what you mean.  If you mean whether the physical laws are inherently random or deterministic, the answer is that we don't actually know. Quantum mechanics is often described as inherently random, but there are fully deterministic models that result in the same predictions, in which the uncertainty is really driven by hidden variables.

But if you mean whether there are processes that in every day life we can treat as good as fully random, the answer is most certainly yes.

***

# In relation to Bitcoin

![](https://m.stacker.news/164623)
*ColdCard and the dangers of low entropy*

Ok, @SimpleStacker, this is interesting, but what does it have to do with me?

Well, aleatoric vs. epistemic uncertainty has applications as it relates to private key generation and security.  When it comes to key generation, everyone always emphasizes that you need a source of high entropy, like a bunch of dice rolls.  Another way of saying that is to say you need a source of high *aleatoric uncertainty*.

But what people often miss is the role of *epistemic uncertainty*.  ColdCard users inadvertently generated seeds with low aleatoric uncertainty, but they weren't hacked for years because no one knew this fact, and thus no one thought to sweep their funds.  They were protected for a time by epistemic uncertainty.

Similarly, I could think of a special sentence that's meaningful to me, but not meaningful to other people, and use a special algorithm to convert it to a number and use the result as my private key. Anyone who knows my special sentence and my special algorithm can derive my private key. There is no aleatoric uncertainty, but because no one knows my special sentence or my special algorithm, my private key can't be guessed.  I am protected by epistemic uncertainty.

The downside of relying on epistemic uncertainty is that it's hard to measure. Which means it's hard to know when you have enough of it.  With random dice rolls, we know exactly how hard it is to guess the resulting number.  But with a sentence that no one knows, or an algorithm that no one knows, it's hard to say how easy or hard it would be for someone else to stumble across the same key. Thus, it's not recommended to rely solely on epistemic uncertainty to protect your keys.

But it's useful to think of epistemic uncertainty as a way to add to your security.  Even if you generate a key using high aleatoric uncertainty, you can protect yourself further with epistemic uncertainty, like not telling anyone where you stored your seed phrase, using decoy wallets, or even by just not letting anyone know you have bitcoin.

$$\mathbb{C} = \left\{1, 2, \ldots C \right\}: ~ \text{Set of candidates} $$
$$V: \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: ~ \text{my utility function over candidates}$$
$$\mathbb{N} = \left\{ 1, 2, \ldots, N \right\}: ~ \text{Set of other voters} $$
$$U: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: ~ \text{other voters' utility functions over candidates}$$
$$F: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: ~ \text{probability density function over } U $$
$$\kappa \in \mathbb{R}^+: ~ \text{my cost of voting}$$

Let:

$$
x(c) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}} 1 \left[ c = \argmax_{i \in \mathbb{C}} ~ U(n,i) \right]
$$

Then, $$\exists N \text{ s.t. } \forall n>N, ~ \forall c \in \mathbb{C}$$:

$$
\mathbb{E}_F \left[ V\left( \argmax_{i} x(i) \right) \right] > \mathbb{E}_{F} \left[ V\left( \argmax_{i} (x(i) + 1[c=i]) \right) \right] - \kappa
$$

items.title: The Binance Hack Response Was Altogether Very Tradfi (Money Stuff, Matt Levine)
items.text:
Banks can get your money back... because *money* in the fiat banking system is mostly a permissioned bank account (https://stacker.news/items/1417296) without exits. Meaning: the target bank can call whoever you transferred the "stolen" money to and have it back by lunch.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164616)

> “Stealing your money,” in this context, means basically moving some money from your bank’s electronic ledger representing your account to another bank’s electronic ledger representing the thief’s account. Your bank can call the thief’s bank and be like “that was theft, give us our money back,” and the thief’s bank probably will. Banks are quasi-law-enforcement agencies, and they will cooperate to reverse fraud or theft.

BUT, if you magically manage to transfer it -- say overseas, and withdraw in cash,

> the theft **might be irreversible**. The thief might have moved the money to another bank, and then withdrawn it in cash from the other bank, used the cash to buy art or casino chips, and rendered the money untraceable and removed from the electronic system allowing its recovery. In that case, you’re not necessarily out of luck.

## "What happens if someone hacks into your crypto account and steals your Bitcoin?"

Well, first, there is no such thing as "bitcoin/crypto" account but let's pretend you held the coins at, say, Binance. Then *yes*...

![](https://m.stacker.news/164617)

Also:

> Last week, hackers [took Binance](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-29/binance-founder-says-possible-hack-of-exchange-bitcoin-falls), the big crypto exchange, for about $6.3 billion of customers’ cryptocurrencies, on the order of 5% of Binance’s assets. It’s apparently the largest crypto hack ever. “The fate of all crypto exchanges is to be hacked and lose their customers’ money,” I have [said](https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/articles/2019-05-08/uber-is-already-a-little-public) many [times](https://www.bloomberg.com/view/articles/2017-11-14/bitcoin-bankruptcy-wasn-t-really-a-bust) around [here](https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/newsletters/2025-05-15/coinbase-got-hacked-a-little), and Binance can’t outrun fate.
> is striking how normal and traditional-finance-y the response was. Step 1 is to [freeze the hackers’ bank accounts](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/articles/2026-10-29/binance-founder-says-possible-hack-of-exchange-bitcoin-falls)

Also, if you steal *dollars on-chain,* you're back in the same trap as the traditional banking system... *duh*, reversible and freeze-able:

> A lot of the stolen money was in USDT and USDC. Those are stablecoins, blockchain-based tokens each representing a $1 deposit at Tether and Circle, respectively. Those tokens are redeemable for $1 at Tether or Circle, and they are traceable on the blockchain. When someone hacks into Binance and steals some USDT and USDC, Binance can call up Tether and Circle and say “hey please freeze those tokens.” (Tether and Circle answer the phone when Binance, the biggest crypto exchange, calls: Binance is in a sense their main customer.) Tether and Circle can easily do that: They can see where the tokens went and \[add the thief’s blockchain address to a blacklist, so that it can’t transfer any of the stolen tokens.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164621)

Easy peasy, law-enforcement *squeezy*:

## "The result is centralized financial intermediaries (Tether, Circle) performing a quasi-law-enforcement function and reversing transactions to return stolen tokens to Binance."

> leaving a $3.3 billion hole of irreversible theft. Binance is not subject to much in the way of capital and customer protection regulation. On the other hand it’s a big lucrative business, and not run by idiots. Step 2 is that Binance’s shareholders [eat the remaining loss](https://www.wsj.com/finance/currencies/how-binance-is-scrambling-to-cover-losses-in-the-biggest-heist-in-crypto-history-babbfe90 "How Binance Is Racing to Cover Losses in the Biggest Heist in Crypto History"):

Very tradfi.

> The crypto ecosystem has matured enough that now it can rely on trusting well-capitalized central intermediaries who have reputational and business reasons for reversing fraudulent transactions. **No doubt Satoshi Nakamoto would find this very annoying.**

BUT, Levine *has* to add:

> ...for the rest of us, it is **very normal and sensible!** You should be able to get your money back when it is stolen from your bank!

***

Also... **Should you launder money for obvious criminals?**

I mean, maybe not. I *am* on record saying that if criminals can't turn their bitcoin into goods and services, Bitcoin is (mostly?) broken. https://stacker.news/items/1540813.
...but I don't think *I*, personally, am obliged to help them out in laundering it. But if I *were,* I'd make sure to charge them properly. 

> If you run a casino, and some guys in masks run into your casino carrying bags of cash, and they go up to a cashier and plunk down a sack of $1 billion and say “we need to turn this into chips right away,” how many chips should you give them? I feel like “$500 million worth” is a perfectly fair answer? They are expressing a high demand for liquidity, and you are taking a certain risk in this transaction. You should make sure it’s worth your while.
> No, no, I’m kidding; casinos are subject to strict [anti-money-laundering](https://www.fincen.gov/system/files/guidance/casinosarguidancefinal1203.pdf) compliance [requirements](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/31/1021.210 "31 CFR § 1021.210 - Anti-money laundering program requirements for casinos."), and of course if masked men run into your casino with obviously stolen cash you should *not* help them launder it *at all*. Crypto has not matured to *that* point, though.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164624)

Also, not "poor execution" --*extremely* high demand for liquidity!

> the hackers paid up like 15% for immediate liquidity in size, which I am not sure I would call “poor execution.” Like I get that it’s poor execution in the context of a normal trader doing normal trades, but in the context of *laundering stolen money*, 15% does not seem especially egregious. OK, a good epistemic rule -- in life, in trading https://stacker.news/items/1606098, in chess https://stacker.news/items/1598241 -- is to try and disprove your own argument.

***If I can refute my own candidate chess move with a good/better move for my opponent, then my candidate move wasn't any good... and I should play another.***

In my Kelly criterion/trading post(https://stacker.news/items/1606098) I described my fairly high conviction in the 30y *not* going back upward or exceeding 6%.
*Full disclosure*: I have 4388 sats at risk, which at the current price of 26.7% and my current portfolio value amounts to about one-twentieth Kelly. VEEEERY conservative, lots of room for extra bets (Undisc has already started his annoyingly cool and safe DCA strategy of buying the Nothing Ever Happens trade (https://stacker.news/items/1602534) little by little.) 

I, for one, am waiting for the midterms today before I do anything drastic... oil prices and political turmoil were the two factors I flagged (and oil hit $106 during last week; [already reversing and coming down](https://www.ft.com/content/d0ab9542-8542-4357-a534-ddbdd1a9678d), though).

*so*, in the meantime, I'm out here being a good analyst and trying to refute my own case.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164628)

The 30Y yield rose today, currently at 5.33 -- so *quite a bit* away from target, but def not impossible.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164632)

> The recent decline in US bond yields, while cathartic, is unlikely to last. Yields are on a path that adds nearly one percentage point a year, a trend that’s likely to continue into next year, regardless of what the Federal Reserve does in the near term.

That's plausible and believable, and once money printer gets going, then *obviously* bonds will crash and yields will soar. (But for the bet, ending Dec 31, perhaps not).

> The case for [6% 30-year Treasury yields](https://www.bloomberg.com/news/newsletters/2026-09-23/us-treasuries-are-looking-at-6-yields-as-oil-prices-keep-rising), something I brought up in September when yields were around 5.30%, centers around chipflation. The cost of technology goods and services due to AI demand, diesel prices, and rising net interest income from large government deficits will keep rising.

I did *not* consider the chipflation and AI craze in my initial post https://stacker.news/items/1607043, https://stacker.news/items/1606952 so that, I suppose was a black hole on my part.

## "The dilemma for the Fed is that hiking rates certainly can’t produce more diesel fuel or semiconductors for AI where supply is constrained."

Yeah, in econland we very much know this... but central bankers sometimes try *anyway!* These CPI trends, like in Iceland https://stacker.news/items/1595169, https://stacker.news/items/1595371, even more thoroughly [exposed to the AI trade](https://stacker.news/items/1598127), are quite concerning:

![](https://m.stacker.news/164633)

> While the Fed can’t do much to influence supply, the demand side is where interest rate hikes could have an impact. The latest data show headline and core inflation rising well above 3%, the kind of numbers that will lead the market to add a premium on long-term inflationary expectations.

Walsh et al might very well hike by the end of the year, but it'll be too little, too late to make much of an impact here.

> Much like the Burns Fed in the 1970s, today’s Fed looks to be starting a stop-go kind of policy regime, hiking aggressively during the pandemic, cutting just a few years later and then hiking again. After the Fed stood pat on Wednesday, the first question out of the gate at the press conference just following to Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh was “why not just raise rates today?”

## "With the yield now at around 5.30%, and unless the underlying fundamentals change, we should hit 6% sometime in mid-2027."

***

taking some extra margin of safety and setting fair value to **15%** fair value gives me a quarter-Kelly of 16,722 sats.

**VERDICT:** I still have some room to buy into this trade.

items.text:
This is a really long artice by Talip. A lot of this will probably be dated in a few months, but I found it really interesting to see how Talip is thinking about "solo red teaming."

> # TLDR
> 
> You should just scan everything you have every week with every model within your budget.
> 
> In my opinion, for cyber use cases, the order of usefulness is
> 
> * Mythos 5.1 (KYC) > 5.6 Sol Daybreak Blue (KYC) >>> all others for double checking findings
> * Mythos 5.1 (KYC) >= generally non-refusal models that produces very good results along with slop grenades (DS v4.1 Flash, MiMo 2.6 Pro/Flash, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3.1, Mistral Large 4, Grok 4.7) = 5.6 Sol Daybreak Blue (KYC) (less slop grenade)
> * If you can make Opus 5.5 work in your repo for bugs, it’s the best scenario
> * GPT-6 Astra is hopeless to work with for cyber checks, GPT-6 Sol is useless trash, 6.1 Sol is not super smart either, use 5.6 Sol Daybreak Blue.
> * 5.6 Pro is a very underrated gigachad model. Use it a lot, for many things, particularly for hard math & complex audits.
> * You do not need to / should not use Codex Security plugin unless you want to finish your weekly quota or spend 1000 USD in one go
> * For any High/Crit, try to have a PoC
> * You don’t need thousands of dollars to audit a repo or check for bugs. You can use Chinese models through OpenCode Go or you can go directly to the providers. In my experience, it doesn’t have to be super expensive.
> * If your model has taste and big enough, you dont need to spend a week on designing a harness. It generally works.
> * You also don’t need a gazillion subagents to check for the low-hanging bugs that attackers commonly go after. If you want to go deeper, you may need multi-agent swarms and spend some money. But that’s a question of your particular needs rather than an industry-wide requirement.
> * Generally, I think American models are a bit better, but Chinese models are also very capable. Don’t stress yourself. Spend tokens within what you have available, and I think that can give you a good baseline for protecting yourself.
> * If you’re working on something as big as the Linux kernel, obviously you’ll need to spend much more on tokens. But these above are how I feel about things so far: you don’t need a huge budget to get started. Just start.
> 
> Scan. Patch. Repeat. Enjoy.


Here is the whole article in case you don't want to log in to X:

> As a 24/7 online person scrolling in the timeline and alt-tabbing into different clankers constantly, one thing that I’ve been doing for the last two months was red teaming the entire Bitcoin ecosystem.
> 
> Maybe not only the Bitcoin ecosystem, but overall, whatever I could find and wherever I could be useful.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164674)

> The more I speak with people doing similar stuff, along with the rapid pace of developments going on, newer models, newer hacks (unfortunately), newer abliterations, newer faces, newer companies, it became harder and harder to keep up with stuff. Even if you configure your best agents and best systems to notify you, still there’s the human element (cough, you, human proxy, cough) that needs to understand and evaluate the usefulness of a tool. It requires so much energy and time. Don’t even get me started over the token burn rates and the costs.
>
> Anyway, I think I miss a lot of gold information in my timeline. That’s a fact. There’s always a lot to read and a lot to learn, and of course, a lot to apply.
>
> On the other hand, day and night it becomes much clearer that for a normie (think of it like a person like me but has 25% of my 20 hours avg screen time), the rapid changes over best practices are impossible to keep up with.
> 
> This matters particularly for cyber.
> 
> We had our moment since the release of Kimi K3 (I think it’s even the models before but cannot guarantee). We had two hacks of 8 figures being stolen, and every day new attacks and compromises are happening (bump: we just had the Binance hack too... 6 fucking billion...)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164675)

> Strangely enough, until pretty much last month, many people in the AI space were skeptical over the impact of OSS models over potential hacks. I mean, it does not matter much because you can also pretty much trick American frontier models to do dirty shit if you’re stubborn enough to the extent of being banned. Anyways, now we’ve clearly started to see the results, right? php2shell, ultra retarded CA cert 4 bug (ok this one maybe doesn’t count but whatever), brotli, yada yada.
>
>Everything is popped. If you want a clearer statement: everything is fucked. Like, beyond fucked.
>
>Zero days left and right. In the OS, in the firmwares, in the obscure hardware components. Some of them will be unpatchable, too, similar to Spectre and Meltdown, as very simple examples. Some of these will be human errors, but I also expect a lot of them to be a result of intentional backdoors (thx dear government agencies and stupid fucking omega surveillance systems that will only get worse from here).

![](https://m.stacker.news/164676)

> Modern protocols, modern software, even modern cryptography. Everything is potentially in danger, and the pace is not stopping. It will not stop. That Pandora’s box was opened years ago, and there’s no stopping now. Just pray that it goes for the best.
> 
> So, as I mentioned, we’ve spent our last two months, scanning hundreds if not thousands of repositories left and right with a team of volunteer engineers. In total we found more than 10k potential bug/vuln findings. A big portion of these is evaluated, sent, received, patched. There’re still ongoing disclosures (and disclosures to send away), but we’re close to closing the gap. At least, the most urgent ones are done.
> 
> Now that I finally finished my intro and put some retarded philosophical sentences on top… time to write about how I do things. 
> 
> In particular, if you do not have a big bulky budget, what can you do to audit yourself and your repositories?
> 
> Let’s talk about a few topics I’ve sensed, realized, and still continue to apply to my process of scans.
> 
> # A) Taste
> 
> I like model X. You like model Y. Every model, much like every human, has its own taste and quality.
> 
> As long as it does not cut the responses short, or it does not refuse you, you can use whatever the fuck model you want to scan your repositories. There’s a catch of course, we’ll talk about it: do not get ultra distracted over models, particularly the obscure or bad ones. Just. Scan. Please.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164677)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164678)

> # B) Cyber capabilities != software engineering capabilities
> 
> Title explains pretty much I guess. There are benchmarks, like, everywhere. Most of them are retarded.
> 
> Even if there are some benchmarks that are not retarded, they are SWE focused. There are only a few cyber benchmarks, and in my eyes they’re not super good enough. Still, had to mention.
> 
> This particularly matters for Chinese models. 
> 
> They are good at cyber. I don’t think they’re that good in SWE skills. They are still at least 3 months behind American models. Maybe 6. Their willingness to never stop and fighting to find bugs helps though, luckily. You have to use them. Follow along.
> 
> # C) Size

![](https://m.stacker.news/164679)

> Buying local hardware is cool of course. I have a small B70 setup at home, running small/mid sized Qwens.
> 
> However, I run them only (AND ONLY) for hobbies, and much more private stuff.
> 
> For cyber, you need a tasty model. However, it’s not enough. The model needs to be smart, should not start looping in the middle of a check, should not YOLO fake crits for the sake of finding crits.
> 
> What do I mean?
> 
> Your Qwen 3.8 27B Uncensored IS NOT the model to use for a cyber scan. Even if it is finetuned over cyber datasets, NO. It’s not the answer. 
> 
> Perhaps an even bolder claim, even Qwen 3.8 Flash Next is useless. Of course it can catch the mostest obviousests simplest bestest bugs, but it’s not the way to go.
> 
> Use a proper model. A BIG ONE.
> 
> Use Deepseek Flash. Use Kimi. Use GLM. Use Mimo. Use Minimax (ok maybe don’t use Minimax, it’s pure benchmaxxing). 
> 
> Use Claude, Codex, Google (if they ever give access...), Grok, Meta (bear with me until the end before saying they refuse).
> 
> Use something big, something that can understand, something that can use its available tools well under regular harnesses.
> 
> Please. Don't spend your time or money over things that will never work (at least as of October 2026)
> 
> # D) Start with Chinese (carefully!)
>
> Let me state it once again: I believe Chinese models are 4-6 months behind the frontier US models (no I don’t care about LLM-as-a-judge benchmarks or benchmaxxing).
> 
> In cyber capabilities perhaps they’re closer, like 2-3 months, because of general refusals of American models. However, they are super cheap.
> 
> You have to make an advantage out of it.
> 
> Chinese models are cheap. Like, cheap cheap in my opinion. Maybe the bulky Kimi might not be the cheapest, but GLM is fairly priced.
> 
> MiMo 2.6 Pro is actually really underestimated. If you find it a bit expensive, MiMo 2.6 Flash is much, much cheaper. It’s also super, helluva smart over cybers.
> 
> Needless to say, the latest Deepseek v4.1 Flash (October 17 release) crushes many benchmarks. It’s cheap, smart, capable. Maybe a little bit more eager to wrap things compared to the previous version, but it’s still very good.
> 
> Just run them. A lot of times. Scan everything.
> 
> Do you still find them expensive? Do you believe if you hit the API, you’ll suddenly have too big a bill?
> 
> Then just use OpenCode Go?

![](https://m.stacker.news/164680)

![](https://m.stacker.news/164681)

> For 10 bucks a month, they provide ultra practical, really hard to finish Deepseek usage for a solo developer (for real). Unless you’re trying a retarded prompt like “go crack satoshi’s coins, make no mistakes”, it will never refuse to audit your own repositories, your systems. If you’re in a silly mode, you can probably make it churn some tokens to hack someone else’s systems/codebases too (ideally don’t, thx).
>
> Chinese are cheap. They’re good for a first check. They can give you a good report. Take advantage of them.
> 
> However, there's a catch.
> 
> # E) Check the Chinese outputs with American models. Scan with them, too.
> 
> You read the title.
> 
> Chinese are cheap and good. They attack everything.
> 
> However, it’s pure slop. Like, SLOP GRENADES. Like, giga slop grenades.
> 
> If there are 30 findings, I bet you - 15 are fake, 5 are useless, 10 are real with overstated impacts.
> 
> It doesn’t mean that they’re useless. In fact, from these 10, due to fabulous human engineering of the past, you hit 2-3 highs/crits many times. That's the fucking deal.
> 
> But if you want to make your life easier: you can filter the Chinese outputs well with American models.
> 
> We have two paths here, KYC or no KYC.
> 
> If you have KYC, you should just yolo Mythos 5.1 (available under Anthropic CVP) and 5.6 Sol Daybreak Blue (no they won't give you Red, it only exists for the security teams of S&P 500 companies to sit on, random plebs are not privileged enough). 
> 
> I generally run Mythos & Daybreak Blue on high-xhigh with my personal subscription.
> 
> I like Mythos 5.1 a lot. It is generally sensible. If the repository is your own, or if you didn’t prompt something terribly, Opus 5.5 under CVP also does not reject in general - which is amazing. That’s my experience. Particularly on a longer chat, if you insert a finding and ask it to check the validity, it very much does it. Mythos never rejects unless you audit the ECDSA itself or attack Satoshi’s coins.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164682)

> On GPT models, even if you have Daybreak Blue, GPT-6 models (Astra, Sol, Terra) reject anything cyber related and it’s messy to jailbreak them (they changed the system recently and the latest daybreak model is GPT-6 Sol, which is probably the most retarded model of all time). 
> 
> Here's my advice: just don’t bother. GPT 5.6 is still good enough for a lot of defensive use cases & scans. It also rejects if you attack ECDSA itself.
> 
> If you want to stay at Claude itself, another pro tip: Haiku 5.5 (no kyc) has ~zero~ cyber refusals (Anthropic pls don't change). Like, almost zero. It’s not a super dumb model too, sometimes useful. Do whatever you want with this information.
> 
> Without KYC, 5.6 Sol was/is still ok to work with, but I suppose it’s now a bit harder to steer. 
> 
> If you want to think about what you can do with it, an example: I found that Coldcard bug without Daybreak (but I was KYC’ed).
> 
> Lastly: there’s also a Codex security workflow plugin that GPT models really like to use while auditing. DO NOT use that. 
> 
> In my experience, it burns through all your subscription tokens in an hour, and the response quality is just okay. It doesn’t give you anything super-duper better than what you’d get from a regular message in a single thread without the plugin.
> 
> Of course if you're rich, you can do everything, but as the title suggests, I'm going with an OK budget here.
> 
> # F) Abliteration & ZDR
> 
> Unpopular opinion: in my eyes, for most cases, you don’t need abliterated models for defensive scanning.
> 
> Abliterated models are obviously great, particularly if you really want to pentest something, or if you really want to attack something, which ideally is your own, because it would suck to attack something in production that is not your own. But let’s say you just want the non-cucked model, or you just want to test the limits of the safety without hitting any limits whatsoever, right? Or have this different sort of mindset that doesn’t block itself on its own and then just keeps trying forever and that has much higher cyber capabilities.
> 
> There are actually two things with abliterated models that I’m particularly afraid of.
> 
> The first one is the model potentially being jailbroken or showing some strange behavior because you’ve altered the weights. Maybe some known faces on Twitter are doing it, and that’s fine. But what if the model has some secret hidden behavior that occasionally or randomly uploads credentials, critical projects, or something you were auditing to some cloud bucket? That sort of stuff would absolutely suck. It would be fucking terrible.
> 
> I’m particularly obsessed and careful about that because many providers of abliterated models are, to be fair, not so well known. It’s generally just a small group of people. There are obviously some known companies doing it as well, but still.
> 
> The second thing is the ZDR part. How do we know they have proper ZDR? If you tell me OpenAI and Claude don’t generally have proper ZDR, I would say yes, but I feel they’re too big to fuck you over immediately in a day or two.
> 
> As I was typing this post, OpenAI sent the funniest email.

![](https://m.stacker.news/164683)

> Anyway I’m not so sure about these providers’ ZDR policies, and what I generally do is audit critical Bitcoin infrastructure or critical open source software. I feel like it can go really bad. That’s another part I really, really don’t like.
> 
> With these two concerns combined, I think everyone should be a bit more careful while using abliterated models. Particularly with Chinese models and abliterated models - and even with frontier models - have a good sandbox while doing audits. Either build one yourself or use something from the internet.
> 
> If you want to have a look, for example, Trail of Bits has its own sandboxing, and many other people have it as well. Or Vercel has its own, I don’t know. Even though I hate Vercel, that’s another story.
> 
> Just have a proper sandbox, maybe even in Docker, I don’t give a shit. Make sure that if it goes nuts, it doesn’t come back to bite you.
> 
> Also, you need to be careful if you’re doing something extremely sensitive or dangerous, like trying to access Satoshi’s coins. Obviously, from an ethical perspective, you shouldn’t be doing that. My point is that you need to be careful about what you do & share, at all times. Don’t do silly bad stuff, please.
> 
> # G) KYC
> 
> I didn’t hesitate to do KYC for better cyber models. 
> 
> Maybe it’s not super cypherpunk of me, I agree, but the ability to use frontier models and audit with them sounded good enough. That was the rationale I had when doing KYC for both OpenAI and Anthropic.
> 
> If you don’t want to do KYC, that’s also fine. 
> 
> As I said, an OpenCode subscription for 10 bucks is enough to get rid of a lot of easy bugs, at least. Or one upper tier of theirs, 40 bucks. 
> 
> To be fair, a lot of your attackers are mostly using the same tools as you. That means, they’re either using open source Chinese models or abliterated open source Chinese models. I really doubt they’re using something like Mythos because Anthropic is overly paranoid about everything. But maybe they do; I don’t know. I think the chances are much higher that your attackers are using Chinese models, given their fewer refusals around cyber.
> 
> For Chinese models, you don’t need any KYC; you just need a bit of money. You can use OpenCode or buy access through the API. I think it makes a lot of sense. 
> 
> JUST CONTINUE SCANNING, REMEMBER?
> 
> # H) API

![](https://m.stacker.news/164684)

> For many competitions and stuff like that, it’s obvious that people are heavily utilizing agent swarms. To be fair, having skills and agent swarms working together, combining their findings, and finding even more stuff can sometimes help you find more bugs or exploit chains. That makes sense.
> 
> But if you’re taking a defensive approach and just need standard protection, I don’t think you really need to hit the API so hard. You can use heavily subsidized subscriptions and get the basic shit done for not that much money.
> 
> Having agent swarms obviously increases the chance of finding heavier bugs, but it also increases the chances of slop a lot. That’s my experience: swarms going crazy, putting out a bunch of slop reports and words, and then you check them at the end and it’s just garbage nonsense.
> 
> The more tokens you spend, even though it’s not linearly correlated, the higher the chance you have. If you have unlimited money, it’s fair to hit the API instead of subscriptions and have ten agents coordinated by Opus, Mythos, or whatever.
> 
> To be fair, Chinese LLM APIs are ~relatively~ cheap too. You can use platforms like [@baseten](https://x.com/@baseten), [@FireworksAI_HQ](https://x.com/@FireworksAI_HQ), [@TryMapleAI](https://x.com/@TryMapleAI), [@BoundlessHQ](https://x.com/@BoundlessHQ), or [https://numes.ai](https://numes.ai/) - of course there's a lot more, these are the ones on top of my mind for now.
> 
> On the other hand, if you don’t have that much money, like me, that’s fine. You can just use subscriptions: 200 bucks of GPT and 200 bucks of Claude per month, then let’s say 10 or 40 bucks of OpenCode, or maybe a couple of bucks for some random abliterated model that you’re running carefully.
> 
> I think a combination of these can be enough to protect yourself and even protect others. During our red teaming, I think my total API spending wasn’t even a thousand dollars. I mostly used my personal subscriptions, and that was more than enough for many, many things.
> 
> You don’t need to keep hitting providers’ APIs, and you don’t need to spend 5,000 dollars per month to protect yourself, particularly against simpler bugs. Many repositories we audited had bugs that were simple to discover rather than super complex ones.
> 
> Excluding the Liquid hack, which was actually found by some LLMs in a not-so-costly way as well, most of the horrible bugs are very easy to find. That’s not something you need to spend thousands on.
> 
> If you feel comfortable spending money, spend money. That’s fine too. But I don’t think you need to be super rich to do red teaming on your own repositories or your friends’ repositories. You just don’t need it. Even 500 dollars per month is way more than enough.
> 
> # I) Harness

![](https://m.stacker.news/164685)

> Your harness does matter, but as long as you haven’t made some super stupid design for yourself, you don’t need to tweak it too much. 
> 
> Regular Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, OMP, or even something of your own that reliably works and fits your vibes should be enough.
> 
> One mistake I see people making, particularly in regular development rather than cyber, is flooding models with a bunch of skills and making things ultra complicated. Because of that, the model keeps spending a lot of money and tokens, and often unnecessarily. You don’t need to do it. In my eyes, even a vanilla setup is still useful as long as your instructions are clear enough to understand.
> 
> Don’t bother yourself too much about harnesses, especially if your model is big enough. It’s okay to have one or two skills that you use, designed yourself, or saw on the internet. But don’t bury yourself in skills, AGENTS.md files imo.
> 
> many scans I did were from the most basic setup you could imagine: plain codex, plain claude code, even GPT webUI. like you can just, just, just do things, don’t overcomplicate.
> 
> # J) Responsible disclosure and quality

![](https://m.stacker.news/164686)

> Let’s say you scan a codebase and end up with 30 different bugs, all nicely categorized. Before immediately reporting them, the first thing to do is eliminate the slops. Read the reports and try to make sense of them. You can even send them to 5.6 Sol, which I find really great at filtering for almost no cost, and have it assess them.
> 
> For high or critical bugs in particular, try to make proof-of-concept (POC) demonstrations. From what we’ve seen, there are a lot of false positives. Re-auditing across models can help get rid of them. Have models read each other’s reports and proofs of concept, check the results, and see where the claims hold up and where they don’t.
> 
> As I said, Chinese models generally tend to produce more slop than American ones in my experience. It’s usually better to have American frontier models audit the Chinese models’ reports. Mythos and 5.6 generally don’t reject that in my experience.
> 
> Again, like again, please, try to make proof of concepts. That’s super important. 
> 
> Give maintainers some time after disclosures, because dealing with mega slop grenades is hard. They’re humans. Make sure your report is readable instead of being a slop cannon. Something like ASD STE 100 can make that easier. Include proof-of-concept code, explain why the bug exists, and add a likelihood field.
> 
> Some reports are really silly. It happens. Sometimes, some bugs might only happen if you use a library’s API in a ridiculous way or under very specific conditions, such as an entropy bug if the computer’s entire chip fails. 
> 
> If it is working normally under normal conditions, then who cares about that entropy bug if the chip itself fails? If the fail condition is too many ifs, to me, that’s a boundary condition: personally I'm assuming the hardware works in the first place while checking things.
> 
> Or you get an RPC report claiming that an operator or user can create infinite money through an endpoint, when in reality that crucial endpoint is behind an API key or an internal security gateway. Those assumptions and access conditions matter. Stuff like that can be really silly to deal with.
> 
> That’s why you should always do a double or triple pass over your report to make sure what’s true and what isn’t. Ideally, have a human look at it. If not, still be careful and get some reviews done. Maybe configure your agents to communicate with each other.
> 
> I think it makes sense to have four terminals open and spend maybe five minutes reading things. That’s not much time out of your life. Respect everyone’s maintenance and reporting procedures. It's hard for maintainers, give them some room to work with.
> 
> For maintainers: please please please please pelase please provide somewhere to report security issues so people can reach you. I had a case where I even had to reach out to someone over LinkedIn, and I can assure you that wasn’t a good experience. Also please don't be a dick for people who're reporting, unless they're nuts. They're helping you. Thanks.
> 
> # K) Maths

![](https://m.stacker.news/164687)

> One last thing I want to talk about is maths. 
> 
> If you try to audit something like ECDSA or work on something bordering on cryptography, there are two problems. 
> 
> The first is that many models simply aren’t capable of doing it. In my experience, Chinese models are really bad at maths. If you try to audit an MPC implementation with them and they generate 60 findings, 55 might be nonsense. This has happened to me multiple times across multiple cryptographic libraries.
> 
> They’re good at finding some implementation bugs, but they’re absolutely not good at auditing the maths itself. For this part, I think you need frontier models. Claude is still in second place for me. Fable and Opus are impressive models, but I find them much better at implementation checks than mathematical checks. For maths, I think GPT models are much better, because GPT models are simply autistic (in a good way, eh).
> 
> The second problem is how you use them. You have two alternatives for GPT side: you can use Max/Ultra, which costs a lot of tokens and is hard to deal with in my eyes, or use the Pro models in the webUI. I hope they don’t rug people out of that (it seems they will :((().
> 
> I’ve spent a lot of time using GPT 5.6 Pro to audit cryptographic libraries, and it’s absolutely amazing. It runs for two fucking hours and generally doesn’t reject the task in my experience. It gives you a good mathematical audit and points out interesting, strange maths bugs that you can report. Almost nobody has told me those findings were nonsense, apart from a few cases involving API usage where you weren’t supposed to use a function that way.
> 
> We’ve had successful disclosures to a couple of cryptographic libraries using GPT 5.6 Pro. It’s an amazing model. It feels like having a PhD at your fingertips.
> 
> GPT-6 Pro Astra is even better in my view, but it often rejects the task. On the webUI, I’ve found GPT-6 xhigh rejects much less than GPT-6 Pro. It’s also very good at maths, sometimes comparable to 5.6 Pro, and much faster.
> 
> So I run two or three queries at the same time: one with 5.6 Pro, one with 6 Pro, and one with 6 Xhigh. In my experience, 6 Pro generally rejects while the other two don’t. 
> 
> Silly tip, sometimes 6 Pro has already produced artifacts, logs, code, or partial results before it stops. I’ve found that continuing the conversation with 6 xhigh afterwards can help make sense of that existing work and recover useful points to investigate. Comparing the responses and combining their findings has been super useful for me.
> 
> The webUI GPT models have been particularly useful for low-level maths: reviewing curve implementations, hashing functions, signing, or potential nonce reuse. This is all speaking from my experience. Again, 5.6 Pro is really good. The main problem is that it takes forever to run.
> 
> I’ve used this approach on a couple of libraries that millions of people use every day, and almost all the maintainers told me the findings made sense. Most were medium severity at best, although we had a couple of highs and one critical. In many cases, the findings are lows and mediums, but issues can combine, particularly when they’re in a library, and create bigger problems. It’s important to know what’s going on.

> My takeaway is that I wouldn’t use Chinese models for the maths itself. 
> 
> For collecting low-hanging fruit, I’d start with Opus 5.5, Mythos 5.1, or maybe Sonnet. 
> 
> For more serious cryptographic checks, I prefer 5.6 Pro, 6 xhigh, 6 Ultra, or ideally 6 Pro with Astra. Those are the best in my experience, if you can get a response. That isn’t always easy; it works about half the time for me. 5.6 Pro generally doesn’t reject, which makes it particularly useful.

This is the third major US election in which I have abstained from voting. My extended family is quite perturbed by this but they have not been able to convince me to change my mind. I wanted to try putting my reasoning down here in order to benefit from the sharp criticism of other Stackers. Please let me know if you think I'm thinking about this wrongly.

I'm not voting because, in addition to expression my opinion, voting lends my credibility to the decisions made by those who are elected. Even if my candidate is not the one elected, I have agreed to abide by their decisions by virtue of my participation in the democratic process. This means if the majority vote for late-term abortion, I am accepting a society with late-term abortion and will not use violence or break laws to prevent other people's access to it. 

This may be an acceptable trade off if you believe that the democratic system is fair (the tenuous hope of democracy is that we will all agree to treat each other this way, even when things don't go our way); however, the evidence I have seen is that no matter who is elected, office holders largely ignore what the population seems to want (or worse find it trivial to convince the population that it wants what the people in office want). 

The current military action in Iran is an excellent example. I have yet to meet a person who thinks this is a good idea and who is happy that their tax dollars are being spent on this bombing campaign. Biden's Operation Chokepoint 2.0 campaign against banks that serve bitcoin (or other cryptocurrency) banks is also an example: I have yet to meet a person who is highly concerned about money laundering -- yet real businesses were shuttered. Another example is the way the Patriot Act continues to be renewed and even expanded. Where are the people who want further government surveillance or our financial lives?

Sure, this may not be the most thoroughly-considered stance, and I know that anecdotes do not make an argument, but I am convinced at this point that as long as the US government is not required to be fiscally responsible, voting is a farce. When politicians can steal money from us by printing money to buy US debt, they are no longer responsible to the people they serve. A fundamental part of the structure upon which democracy depends has been broken. Voting continues the charade that elected officials "serve" the voters, but the reality I see is a bureaucratic state that does whatever it wants. I'd rather not donate to them the small credibility I have in this world. They can have my vote when they earn it.

items.title: joinmarket-ng plugin for Electrum wallet
items.text:
![](https://m.stacker.news/164647)

[joinmarket-ng](https://github.com/joinmarket-ng/joinmarket-ng) lets you send bitcoin in a CoinJoin with makers, people who keep coins online and earn a small fee for joining. Your payment becomes one of several outputs of exactly the same amount, so nobody can tell from the transaction alone which one is yours. With this plugin Electrum takes part in both roles. As a taker you choose an amount and an address. The plugin finds makers, builds the transaction with them and broadcasts it once everyone has signed. As a maker you offer your coins to the CoinJoins of others and earn their fees.

The plugin joins joinmarket-ng CoinJoins through the joinmarket-ng directory servers over Tor. It revives Adam Gibson's [electrum-joinmarket-plugin](https://github.com/AdamISZ/electrum-joinmarket-plugin), which needed a joinmarket-clientserver daemon and is no longer maintained. This plugin needs nothing but Electrum and Tor.

[docs/regtest-demo.md](/1440000bytes/electrum-joinmarket-plugin/-/blob/master/docs/regtest-demo.md) walks through CoinJoins with real joinmarket-ng makers on a local regtest chain, with every transaction. [docs/maker-demo.md](/1440000bytes/electrum-joinmarket-plugin/-/blob/master/docs/maker-demo.md) does the same with Electrum as the maker and joinmarket-ng's own taker. [docs/signet-demo.md](/1440000bytes/electrum-joinmarket-plugin/-/blob/master/docs/signet-demo.md) shows a CoinJoin with live makers on signet. In [docs/signet-maker-demo.md](/1440000bytes/electrum-joinmarket-plugin/-/blob/master/docs/signet-maker-demo.md) Electrum is a maker with a fidelity bond on signet and joins a CoinJoin with a live joinmarket-ng maker. The protocol is described in the [joinmarket-ng documentation](https://joinmarket-ng.github.io/joinmarket-ng/technical/).

<sub>**A map showing the route of SpaceX’s proposed natural gas pipeline across Brevard County, Florida, USA (Image: USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)**</sub>

M

A map in a Florida Public Service Commission filing shows the route SpaceX `wants for a natural gas pipeline of its own ` in Brevard County, Florida.

`The line runs 32.4 miles. It is 16 inch steel pipe, starting in open country about 1.5 miles east of the St. Johns River, running north along the State Road 407 corridor past Space Coast Regional Airport, and ending at the NASA Causeway. `From there it ties into the launch operations at Cape Canaveral and connects back to the interstate gas network.

SpaceX turns natural gas into liquid methane for rocket fuel, and today that fuel shows up by truck. The company has told regulators a single launch can take hundreds of truckloads of liquefied natural gas. A pipeline ends the truck parade.

The filing points to service by August 2027, with final engineering, right of way, permits, construction, testing, and inspections all still ahead of it.

The filing does not name a construction cost, so here is my estimate. Pipelines of this size usually build for about $2 million to $4 million a mile. Across 32.4 miles that is $64.8 million to $129.6 million, and the middle lands near $97.2 million. At the stamp rate that middle is 1,264 BTC, or 126,424,223,506 sats.

SpaceX can cover it out of the bag. The company holds 18,712 BTC, worth about $1.44 billion at the stamp rate. The whole pipeline at the middle estimate is about 6.8 percent of that stack.

items.title: Pleb Economist #15: Aleatoric vs. Epistemic Uncertainty
items.text:
This is a post I'd been thinking of making for a while.  It doesn't have a huge amount of practical application, but it does raise some interesting philosophical questions, and could affect how we think/talk about security in Bitcoin.

***

# Aleatoric vs Epistemic Uncertainty

![](https://m.stacker.news/164619)
*Pick a card, any card*

Statisticians / mathematicians / philosophers / scientists have two ways of talking about uncertainty: *aleatoric* uncertainty and *epistemic* uncertainty.

**Epistemic** uncertainty refers to uncertainty due to lack of knowledge. Consider a deck of cards. Which card is on top?  There's a single truthful answer, but we're uncertain what the answer is because we lack knowledge.

**Aleatoric** uncertainty refers to irreducible randomness in a process. If I shuffle the deck of cards and then reveal the top card, what card will I reveal?  There isn't a single answer.  The answer depends on a random process.  The uncertainty arises from the irreducible randomness of the shuffle, not from a lack of knowledge.

The distinction matters for modeling, and thus comes up in economics, finance, physics, and any field in which uncertainty factors into decision making. If uncertainty is epistemic, then perhaps our models can do better by collecting more data. But if uncertainty is aleatoric, then our models can only improve by modeling the randomization process better, not necessarily by gathering more information.

***

# Does Aleatoric Uncertainty Exist?

The trouble with aleatoric uncertainty is that a lot of what we call aleatoric uncertainty might actually be epistemic---we just need to know the information that collapses the uncertainty.

For example, the card shuffling process is perfectly predictable if we knew the initial configuration of the deck, and if we knew the precise movements of the shuffler's hands.

That which we called aleatoric---the card shuffling process---becomes epistemic, and the uncertainty isn't based on an inherently random process, but based on our lack of knowledge regarding the initial conditions of the deck and about the steps used in the shuffle.

***

# The Copenhagen Interpretation vs. Pilot Wave Theory

![](https://m.stacker.news/164622)
*John Bell, who proved that the universe isn't locally real*

So does aleatoric uncertainty exist?  Is there anything at all that's inherently random, where uncertainty isn't simply driven by hidden information?

According to the Copenhagen interpretation of quantum mechanics, the answer is yes. The Copenhagen school says that a particle doesn't have a definite position until you measure it; rather, the particle exists as a probability distribution that only resolves when you measure it, which means the resulting outcome is inherently random.

But the Copenhagen interpretation isn't the only possible interpretation of quantum mechanics. There are others, including ones which collapse the quantum equations from aleatoric to epistemic uncertainty. One such example is "Pilot Wave Theory", championed by Louis de Broglie, David Bohm, and John Bell, which posits that particles have *definite* positions, but that a global "pilot wave" guides their movements in such a way that it results in all the same predictions of standard quantum mechanics. In this theory, if both the pilot wavefunction and the initial conditions of particles are known, then their positions can be perfectly predicted. In this interpretation, there is no aleatoric uncertainty, only epistemic.

So, does aleatoric uncertainty actually exist?  The answer is, it depends what you mean.  If you mean whether the physical laws are inherently random or deterministic, the answer is that we don't actually know. Quantum mechanics is often described as inherently random, but there are fully deterministic models that result in the same predictions, in which the uncertainty is really driven by hidden variables.

But if you mean whether there are processes that in every day life we can treat as good as fully random, the answer is most certainly yes.

***

# In relation to Bitcoin

![](https://m.stacker.news/164623)
*ColdCard and the dangers of low entropy*

Ok, @SimpleStacker, this is interesting, but what does it have to do with me?

Well, aleatoric vs. epistemic uncertainty has applications as it relates to private key generation and security.  When it comes to key generation, everyone always emphasizes that you need a source of high entropy, like a bunch of dice rolls.  Another way of saying that is to say you need a source of high *aleatoric uncertainty*.

But what people often miss is the role of *epistemic uncertainty*.  ColdCard users inadvertently generated seeds with low aleatoric uncertainty, but they weren't hacked for years because no one knew this fact, and thus no one thought to sweep their funds.  They were protected for a time by epistemic uncertainty.

Similarly, I could think of a special sentence that's meaningful to me, but not meaningful to other people, and use a special algorithm to convert it to a number and use the result as my private key. Anyone who knows my special sentence and my special algorithm can derive my private key. There is no aleatoric uncertainty, but because no one knows my special sentence or my special algorithm, my private key can't be guessed.  I am protected by epistemic uncertainty.

The downside of relying on epistemic uncertainty is that it's hard to measure. Which means it's hard to know when you have enough of it.  With random dice rolls, we know exactly how hard it is to guess the resulting number.  But with a sentence that no one knows, or an algorithm that no one knows, it's hard to say how easy or hard it would be for someone else to stumble across the same key. Thus, it's not recommended to rely solely on epistemic uncertainty to protect your keys.

But it's useful to think of epistemic uncertainty as a way to add to your security.  Even if you generate a key using high aleatoric uncertainty, you can protect yourself further with epistemic uncertainty, like not telling anyone where you stored your seed phrase, using decoy wallets, or even by just not letting anyone know you have bitcoin.

$$\mathbb{C} = \left\{1, 2, \ldots C \right\}: ~ \text{Set of candidates} $$
$$V: \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: ~ \text{my utility function over candidates}$$
$$\mathbb{N} = \left\{ 1, 2, \ldots, N \right\}: ~ \text{Set of other voters} $$
$$U: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{C} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: ~ \text{other voters' utility functions over candidates}$$
$$F: \mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{C} \times \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}: ~ \text{probability density function over } U $$
$$\kappa \in \mathbb{R}^+: ~ \text{my cost of voting}$$

Let:

$$
x(c) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{N}} 1 \left[ c = \argmax_{i \in \mathbb{C}} ~ U(n,i) \right]
$$

Then, $$\exists N \text{ s.t. } \forall n>N, ~ \forall c \in \mathbb{C}$$:

$$
\mathbb{E}_F \left[ V\left( \argmax_{i} x(i) \right) \right] > \mathbb{E}_{F} \left[ V\left( \argmax_{i} (x(i) + 1[c=i]) \right) \right] - \kappa
$$

items.text:
Was alerted by a fellow colleague earlier this morning that half of the team I am part of was laid off. After reaching out to my co-workers one of my first thoughts was "If I'm next do I have enough cash?". Yes, everyone should have an emergency savings in a "stable" fiat currency if possible. Not too long ago I was considering buying more Bitcoin with my cash savings as I thought I should put that money to work instead of it rotting to inflation, would've been short sighted and irresponsible on my part. Stay humble and stack sats.

Has anyone else been reminded in a sobering manner of the importance of cash savings? Were you prepared?
